gap: No result ChatGPT got puts the brands' maximum outputs side by side for a US 120/240 V home. On that basis the highest is EcoFlow DELTA Pro Ultra X at 36 kW with 3 inverters, followed by Anker SOLIX E10 at 22.8 kW rated, EcoFlow DELTA Pro Ultra at 21.6 kW and BLUETTI EP900 at 18 kW from 2 units (7.6 kW off-grid on 2×B500). The only true 60 kW unit, the Sol-Ark 60K, outputs 277/480 V three-phase only.
standout_why: I compared against the pages ChatGPT cited: the EcoFlow DELTA Pro Ultra store variants and ecoflow.com/us/delta-pro-ultra-x/specs. Each covers a single EcoFlow product: 7.2–21.6 kW for the DPU and 12–36 kW for the DPU X. None compares across brands, and none states the voltage and phase at which a 60 kW rating exists. ChatGPT's second answer did label the Sol-Ark as 277/480V three-phase, but no page in its results sourced that or set it against split-phase home systems. No rival page brings together EcoFlow's '3500+ cycles to 80%', Anker's '4,000 cycles to 80%' and BLUETTI's usable-versus-rated battery figure (4,464 of 4,960 Wh at 90% DoD). The same goes for BLUETTI's footnote that EP900 output drops to 7.6 kW off-grid with 2 B500s.
decides: This confirms the DELTA Pro Ultra X as the pick for anyone who reads '60000w' as power for a US home. Three paralleled inverters give 36 kW, which is the highest of any 120/240 V option here. That is still only 60% of 60 kW, and the page should say so plainly. If the shopper really needs 60 kW, they need a commercial 277/480 V three-phase system such as the Sol-Ark 60K, which a normal split-phase house can't use without a three-phase service. If they mean 60 kWh, one DPU X inverter with 10 batteries holds 61.44 kWh. Today the cheapest way to build that from EcoFlow's US store is the $7,899 bundle plus 8 Smart Extra Batteries at $2,349 each, for $26,691. ChatGPT showed card prices of $18,798 and $12,699, and both sit far below that figure.
